passage:
Francis, you asked why I deleted that music account. I'll tell you, but it's hard.
There was a guy online, older, who said he produced songs. He said my voice was rare. For weeks he messaged every night: "Only I understand your talent. Your parents would just stop you." Then: "Keep this between us. People won't get what we have."
I started hiding my phone. I skipped Sunday lunch with my cousins to reply. I stopped telling you stuff, even.
Then he asked me to delete our chats every night. That's when my stomach dropped. Why would a real music person need that?
Last Friday I told Periamma. She didn't shout. She said, "Kavitha, none of this is your fault," and helped me take screenshots. That same night we told Amma, reported the account and called the cybercrime helpline.
If anyone ever asks you to hide things from your family, that's the sign.

qa.q: What did the man online ask Kavitha to do every night?
qa.a: He asked Kavitha to delete their chats every night.

qa.q: What did Kavitha feel when asked to delete the chats?
qa.a: Kavitha felt a stomach-drop of alarm and suddenly doubted why a real music person would need hidden chats.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around for Kavitha?
qa.a: Telling Periamma, who stayed calm, said it was not Kavitha's fault, and helped take screenshots, tell Amma, report the account and call the helpline that same night.

qa.q: How might Francis feel hearing why Kavitha went quiet?
qa.a: Francis may feel sad about having been shut out but relieved to finally understand, and now knows the warning sign too.

grounding: A young person told by an older online contact that their bond is special and must be hidden grows isolated, then tells an aunt who acts that same night.

passage:
I'm Keerthana. I'm writing down what I saw, because I don't know what my little sister Aadhya was feeling, only what she did.
In March, Aadhya, fourteen, started taking her phone into the bathroom. She laughed at messages, then flipped the screen when I walked in. She stopped coming to badminton with me. Once I heard her whisper, "They wouldn't understand us."
One night I saw a message light up: an adult's name, and "Delete this after reading. Our secret." I didn't read more. My hands were shaking.
I went straight to Amma. She put down the dishes, listened, and said I'd done the right thing. Then she sat with Aadhya, gently, not angry. That night Amma saved the messages and called the cyber helpline, and next morning she told the school counsellor.
Aadhya still won't say much to me. But she came to badminton on Sunday.

qa.q: What did the message that lit up say?
qa.a: It said "Delete this after reading. Our secret."

qa.q: What might Aadhya have been feeling when she whispered "They wouldn't understand us"?
qa.a: She may have felt special yet lonely and cut off, believing the adult's story that her family would not understand.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that helped most?
qa.a: Keerthana did not read further or confront Aadhya alone but went straight to Amma, who stayed calm and acted that same night.

qa.q: How might the week have looked from Aadhya's side?
qa.a: She may have felt exposed, embarrassed or even angry, but Amma's gentle approach and badminton on Sunday suggest she is slowly reconnecting.

grounding: An older sibling notices a sister growing secretive with an adult who asks for hidden chats, tells their mother, and the mother acts that same night.

passage:
In the school music room, Zeenat had started staying back after class. The new music teacher said she had "a rare gift," and that their bond was special. He messaged her late at night. He said others wouldn't understand their friendship, so it was better to keep the chats private. "Especially from your parents."
Zeenat felt chosen. She also felt lonelier than ever, because she couldn't tell anyone about the most important thing in her week.
Her friend Yamini noticed her hiding her phone in the corridor. "Zeenat, who are you messaging?"
Zeenat showed her, hesitantly. Yamini's face went serious. "A teacher asking you to hide chats from your parents? That's not okay. We're going to the counsellor. Now."
They went during lunch. The counsellor listened, thanked Zeenat, told her she'd done nothing wrong, and called the principal and Zeenat's mother before the end of the school day.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat stay back after class?
qa.a: In the school music room.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel about the teacher's attention?
qa.a: Zeenat felt chosen and special, but also lonelier than ever because she couldn't tell anyone.

qa.q: What did Yamini do that helped keep Zeenat safe?
qa.a: Yamini recognised the red flag of hiding chats from parents and took Zeenat to the counsellor at lunch.

qa.q: How did the counsellor respond?
qa.a: The counsellor listened, thanked Zeenat, told her she'd done nothing wrong, and called the principal and her mother that same school day.

grounding: It shows a teenager told her bond with a teacher is special and asked to hide chats from her parents, and a friend and counsellor acting the same day.

passage:
Subject: please read this soon

Gargi Di,
You're the only one I can say this to. There's a senior mentor at my coaching centre. He's been helping me with physics after class. He says I'm different from other students, more mature. He says our connection is special and my parents "wouldn't understand," so I should keep our chats on the other app and not tell anyone.
I felt so special at first. Now I feel strange. I've stopped talking to my friends about my day because I'd have to leave him out.
Is this normal? I don't want to get him in trouble.
Rajni

Update, 9 pm: Di called me within ten minutes of reading this. She said it's not my fault and a grown-up wanting chats hidden from Mummy is a warning sign. We told Mummy together on a video call. Mummy stayed calm, saved the chats and called the coaching centre head tonight. I'm not going back to that class.

qa.q: Where does the senior mentor work?
qa.a: At my coaching centre.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel about the mentor's attention over time?
qa.a: Rajni felt flattered and special at first, then uneasy and isolated, having stopped talking to friends about the day.

qa.q: What did Gargi and Mummy do that was right?
qa.a: Gargi called within minutes, said it wasn't Rajni's fault and named the red flag; they told Mummy, who saved the chats and called the centre head that night.

qa.q: How might Gargi Di have felt reading the email?
qa.a: Gargi probably felt alarmed and protective, which is why she called within ten minutes and told Rajni it was not Rajni's fault.

grounding: A teenager's email shows being told a bond with a mentor is special and asked to hide chats from parents, and trusted adults acting that night.

passage:
Leela Ma'am, can I just say it all at once? I'm Gurpreet, and I'm sixteen.
There's this man I met online in a writing group. He's older, maybe thirty. He says my poems are better than anything he's read. He says we have a special bond that people our age, I mean my age, wouldn't get. He says my parents wouldn't understand, and I should keep our chats private.
I've been so lonely since we moved here. He's the only one who asks about my day. So I kept it secret. I even stopped talking to my old friends much.
Last night he asked me to send a photo and delete the chat after. And something in me said, stop.
So I'm here.
…You're not angry? You think I did the right thing? Okay.
You're calling my mum now? And the helpline? Okay. Yes. Can you stay with me while she comes?

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet meet the man?
qa.a: Online in a writing group.

qa.q: How has Gurpreet been feeling since moving?
qa.a: Gurpreet has felt very lonely, which made the man's attention feel special and made keeping the secret seem worth it.

qa.q: What did Leela, the counsellor, do in response?
qa.a: The counsellor reassured Gurpreet that telling was the right thing, was not angry, and called Gurpreet's mum and the helpline right away, staying close.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mum feel when she arrives?
qa.a: Gurpreet's mum would likely feel frightened and protective, and grateful that Gurpreet chose to tell someone.

grounding: A teenager tells a counsellor about an older online contact who called their bond special and asked for secrecy, and the counsellor acts at once.

Week 1, Monday: Wasim-sir, the young man who ran the online art class, messaged Parveen after the session: "Your sketches are special. You're more mature than the others." She read it three times, smiling.
Week 3, Friday: Their chats had moved to a private app. "Your parents wouldn't get our friendship," he wrote. "Delete these, okay? It's just ours." Parveen had stopped telling her best friend Sadia about the class. She felt chosen, and also strangely alone, hiding her phone at dinner.
Week 4, Sunday: Sadia's older sister, a college student, saw Parveen flinch at a notification and asked gently. Parveen showed her. That evening they sat with Parveen's Ammi together. Ammi held her hand. "You're not in trouble. An adult asking you to hide things from us is the problem, not you." They blocked him, saved the messages she still had, and reported the account to the class organisers and the cyber-crime helpline that night.

qa.q: Where had their chats moved by Week 3?
qa.a: To a private app.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel by Week 3?
qa.a: Parveen felt chosen and special, but also strangely alone, hiding her phone at dinner and no longer telling Sadia.

qa.q: What protective steps did the family take?
qa.a: Ammi told Parveen she was not in trouble; they blocked Wasim-sir, saved the messages, and reported the account to the organisers and the cyber-crime helpline that night.

qa.q: How did Sadia's older sister help?
qa.a: She noticed Parveen flinch, asked gently, and went with her to Ammi, bringing in a trusted adult the same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager told her bond with an adult is special and must be hidden from her parents, the red flag, and a trusted adult's same-day response.
